newsitem.title: THAILAND: Explosive week ahead as Thai PM readies for debate.
newsitem.headline: Explosive week ahead as Thai PM readies for debate.

text.p: Thailand is in for a politically explosive week as its premier prepares for a no-confidence debate in parliament which might unseat him or even force fresh general elections, analysts said on Sunday.
Debate on an opposition-led no-confidence vote against Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa is due to begin on Wednesday.
It accuses him, among other things, of incompetence, economic mismanagement and plagiarism in his thesis for a master's law degree and is expected to last two to three days.
Banharn, who has denied the accusations and vowed to fight them, faces the toughest political fight of his career, political analysts and diplomats told Reuters.
Cracks have begun to appear within his six-party, 14-month-old coalition government as some partners in his administration are wavering in their support, they said.

To add to Banharn's woes, the formerly robust economy has begun to sputter. The stock market is near three-year lows, growth in exports is running flat this year and the baht has become the target of devaluation rumours.
He also faces a hostile local press.
Banharn's coalition controls 209 of the 391 seats in parliament and some analysts predict his allies could support him through the no-confidence vote to save the government.

"Coalition partners have already promised to vote in support of him. But I think there will be big changes after the debate," Sanoh Thienthong, secretary general of Banharn's main Chart Thai party, said.

Other options were for Banharn to remain until his coalition disintegrates, dissolve parliament ahead of the debate and force fresh elections, step down before the no-confidence vote or agree with coalition partners to hand over his post to another acceptable politician, they said.
"Anything can happen. I see things getting worse for the PM whose credibility is very low. A fresh election cannot be ruled out," said an Asian diplomat who declined to be named.

Some cabinet ministers, like outspoken Justice Minister Chalerm Yoobumrung, have told reporters Banharn's departure and the formation of a government including unelected professionals to run the economy could be a way out of current problems.
Trairong Suwannakiri, deputy leader of the main opposition Democrat Party, called on Banharn to step down or be ruined by accusations that would be made at the no-confidence debate.

"Many people want to change the prime minister, not the government," said political analyst Likit Kraivixien. "Chances are that there might not be a no-confidence debate this week and the premier could step down and dissolve parliament."

But Banharn's trump card is the fact that he can dissolve parliament, which many of his government allies who enjoy the trappings of power are against. "He could do that if he finds he cannot trust his allies anymore," said the diplomat.
Political scientists Somchai Pakapakwivat of Thammasart University and Assadang Panikabutra of Ramkhamhaeng University said it was likely Banharn would step down either before or after the debate.

Analysts said that in the event of Banharn stepping down without dissolving parliament, then possible front runners to replace him were Deputy Prime Minister Amnuay Viravan of the small Nam Thai Party or even former premier Chatichai Choonhavan, who was ousted from power by the military in 1991.
Technocrat Amnuay currently looks after economic and foreign affairs. Chatichai heads the opposition Chart Pattana party.
Analysts said another man to watch was Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh who leads senior coalition partner, the New Aspiration Party, and has much influence in government.

In past weeks senior military officers have stressed the armed forces will stay out of politics. The military has launched 17 coups or coup attempts since 1932 when Thailand switched to a constitutional monarchy from absolute monachy.
